diagram_name: Where Is It on the Hype Cycle?
chapter_title: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
learning_objective: The learner will classify eight events in the history of educational technology by the stage of the hype cycle they illustrate, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** where-on-hype-cycle
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify eight events in the history of educational technology by the stage of the hype cycle they illustrate, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** the five stages of the hype cycle, peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, plateau of productivity, EdTech hype waves (all defined in the section "The Hype Cycle and Educational Technology" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 8 events in one of five stage bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct stage" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the stage definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) The trough means a technology has failed. (2) The peak is when a technology is most useful. (3) Every technology follows the cycle exactly. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying events by the pattern of expectations they show, rather than by the technology's quality, makes the learner use the cycle as a lens. Events from different technologies show the same shape recurring. **Content:** Five stages with definitions on request: | Stage | Definition shown | |---|---| | Innovation trigger | A breakthrough or launch sparks interest | | Peak of inflated expectations | Publicity and expectations exceed what the technology can do | | Trough of disillusionment | Failures meet the inflated expectations and interest falls | | Slope of enlightenment | Experiments clarify what the technology is good for | | Plateau of productivity | The technology is understood and used for what it does well | Eight events: | # | Event shown to the learner | Correct stage | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | In November 2012 a major newspaper calls the year "the year of the MOOC," and universities rush to offer free online courses. | Peak of inflated expectations | Publicity and expectations are at their highest. | | 2 | In 2013 a leading MOOC founder says that much of the product is "lousy," and completion rates are often under ten percent. | Trough of disillusionment | Failures meet the inflated expectations. | | 3 | Online courses settle into a useful niche in professional and continuing education, with clear uses. | Plateau of productivity | The technology is understood and used for what it does well. | | 4 | In 2013 a large district announces a plan to give every student a tablet. | Peak of inflated expectations | A large rollout is announced on the strength of expectations. | | 5 | The tablet plan is cancelled after technical problems, weak curriculum, and a contract scandal. | Trough of disillusionment | The failures meet the inflated expectations. | | 6 | A general-purpose AI chatbot is released to the public in November 2022 and attracts enormous attention. | Innovation trigger | A breakthrough product sparks interest. | | 7 | Randomized studies show a guided AI tutor helps and open chatbot access harms later exam scores. | Slope of enlightenment | Experiments clarify what works and why. | | 8 | A few teachers, after the 1980s computer boom, continue experimenting with computers for programming and writing and develop effective practices. | Slope of enlightenment | A smaller group learns what the technology is good for after the hype fades. | **Provenance:** The stages follow the Gartner hype cycle as described in the chapter. The events are drawn from the chapter and Chapters 3 and 11; the sim must label the stage assignments "A reading of the evidence, not a measurement." The MOOC and tablet events should be checked against the sources before publishing. **Rules:** Each event has exactly one correct stage, given in Content. An event is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one event at a time and the five stages. 2. The learner places the event and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct stage and reason are shown. 4. After all 8 events, the sim shows the score and the events arranged along the cycle. 5. The learner should notice that the MOOC and the tablet stories follow the same shape, and that the trough is followed by learning, not only abandonment. **Feedback:** 8 events, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [stage]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the stage]." After the second attempt the correct stage is revealed and the event counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can read the hype cycle in a story." For a score < 7: "Review the five stages and try again; the events will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Event 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the five stages, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which stage of the hype cycle does this event show?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter names five stages of the hype cycle and uses the MOOC wave of 2012 to 2013, the Los Angeles tablet rollout of 2013, and the 2022 chatbot release as examples. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.
